title: Fractions Worksheets: Halves, Thirds, and Fourths
intro: Make equal-area parts, then shade one. A fraction label and a correctly partitioned drawing should tell the same story.
html:
Equal parts must have equal area

A rectangle cut into two pieces does not always show halves. Each piece must cover the same amount of the rectangle. Draw a line halfway across a paper rectangle, fold to compare the pieces, and discuss whether they match.

Name one part

Two equal parts make halves: one part is one half, written 1/2. Three equal parts make thirds: one is one third, written 1/3. Four equal parts make fourths, also called quarters: one is one fourth, written 1/4. Read these names aloud before writing the fraction.

Three equal parts need two dividing lines.

To make three equal strips, mark about one third and two thirds of the rectangle's width. Draw a straight line at each mark, then shade one strip. Count the spaces, not the lines.

Try different partitions

Four equal strips can show fourths. A line through the middle in each direction can also make four equal smaller rectangles. The worksheet does not require one particular arrangement. Check equal area and the requested number of parts.

If the child counts dividing lines instead of parts: point inside each separate region while counting. A rectangle with three dividing lines across its full height has four strips, not three.

Shade exactly one part

After checking the partition, shade one entire region. Shading two of four regions does not show the one fourth requested here. Keep the shading inside the selected region so the boundaries remain clear.

Check the drawing, not just the fraction

A written 1/3 does not prove that three equal parts were drawn. Check that the parts fill the original rectangle without gaps or overlaps, have equal areas, and that exactly one is shaded. Small drawing inaccuracies are an opportunity to compare and adjust, rather than to dismiss the child's understanding.

About these three activities

Each sheet asks for halves, thirds, and fourths once, using the same original rectangle shape. The answer key gives checking guidance rather than a single completed drawing, because more than one partition can be correct. New numbers does not change these three fixed tasks.

This practice uses rectangles only. It does not assess circles or all ways that differently shaped pieces can have equal area. The fraction labels support naming the parts; fraction arithmetic is not required.
